text:
Mia (support): FYI escalation from Acme — they see p99 regressions on streaming responses vs non-streaming. TTFB looks fine but total completion time spikes (users see long pauses between chunks). Happened starting ~2024-11-02 20:12 UTC after yesterday's runtime deploy. They attached a small repro and a trace.

Mia (support): Repro steps they sent (curl):
```
curl -v -H \"Authorization: Bearer $KEY\" \"https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat.stream\" \\\n  -d '{"model":"redwood-1-small","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"count to 50, one number per chunk"}],"stream":true}' 
```
They say first chunk arrives immediately, then later chunks are clumped — p95 ok but p99 high.

Alex (eng-runtime): Can you paste the request-id/traces? Also which region/model? My gut: either our stream.flush_delay got tuned up or some proxy is coalescing small writes. Could also be client-side buffering (node/curl behavior).

Mia (support): Request-id: "rid=acme-20241102-7221". Region: us-west-2, model redwood-1-small. Trace: https://traces.redwood/internal/acme-20241102-7221 (internal).

Ravi (sre): I pulled the edge trace. Connection stayed open, lots of small write syscalls from runtime but there are long gaps at the proxy layer. Header shows `Via: nginx/1.22` and we have `proxy_buffering` defaulted to `on` for that virtual host. That will coalesce small chunks into larger TCP frames. For streaming endpoints we usually set `proxy_buffering off` (we do for SSE but this path might have reverted).

Jordan (eng-platform): I just grep'd config history — there was a change in our configmap last night: stream.flush_ms went from 10 -> 30 to reduce network chatter (commit 9f3a4b). Diff snippet:
```diff
- stream.flush_ms: 10
+ stream.flush_ms: 30  # reduce tiny writes during high qps
```
That explains larger intervals between flushes at the runtime. Combined with proxy buffering on the edge that'll make chunks even rarer.

Alex (eng-runtime): Nice catch. Two independent levers: runtime flush delay and proxy buffering. Also worth validating client-side: some runtimes (node's http) buffer until newline or until buffer hits N bytes. Ask Acme to try `curl -N` or `curl --no-buffer` and see.

Mia (support): I asked customer to run `curl -N` and to try a non-streaming call for baseline. They ran both and returned this snippet: first chunk at ~10ms, then pauses ~200-800ms between subsequent chunks; non-streaming total time was consistently lower for the same payload. They also tried a node fetch client (their webapp) and saw even longer pauses — likely buffering.

Ravi (sre): From edge logs the `nginx` proxy had these metrics around the incident window: `proxy_buffers_used` spiked and `proxy_upstream_time` shows delays aligning with our flush_ms window. Actionable short-term: set `proxy_buffering off` on streaming route to avoid coalescing. Longer-term: ensure our platform sets the right headers for `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` for all streaming endpoints.

Alex (eng-runtime): I can put a quick runtime canary to revert `stream.flush_ms` -> 10 and add a feature flag `disable_chunk_coalesce=true` that immediately flushes small KV writes. Also we should add a per-route metric: time-between-chunks histogram, so we can detect client vs server vs proxy delays.

Jordan (eng-platform): Sounds good. Proposed mitigation plan:
- immediate: platform to toggle `proxy_buffering off` for `/v1/chat.stream` on edge (5min change window)
- immediate: runtime canary (5%) revert `stream.flush_ms` to 10 for canary traffic and enable `disable_chunk_coalesce`
- monitor: per-route p50/p95/p99 of time-between-chunks and completion time for 1h before/after
- medium: add HTTP header `X-Accel-Buffering: no` at ingress and validate with tests
- long: autodetect client buffering (via initial chunk size patterns) and fall back to non-streaming for affected clients after threshold

Alex (eng-runtime): Example runtime debug commands:
```bash
# turn on debug logging for streams on an instance
kubectl exec -it runtime-pod-abc -- sh -c \"export RUNTIME_STREAM_LOG=debug && kill -SIGUSR1 1\"
# run a synthetic:
wrk -t2 -c10 -d30s --script=streaming.lua https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat.stream
```
Also to repro client buffering locally: `curl -N` vs `node --version` + simple fetch script.

Mia (support): I initiated the platform change with Jordan and pinged Acme with repro tips (`curl -N`, node fetch small-chunk flush). They want a timeline. I'll coordinate canary acceptance and share results.

deploy-bot: Canary rollout started: config=runtime.stream.flush_ms reverted->10 (canary=5%).

Ravi (sre): After canary started, edge metrics show chunk intervals tightened for canary traffic. Will monitor p99 for the customer homed to canary. If stable -> escalate canary to 25% then global. Also keep `proxy_buffering off` only for streaming path to avoid regressions for other traffic.

Alex (eng-runtime): Long-term TODOs I added to runtime backlog: better defaults for flush_ms per model/seq-len, adaptive flush based on downstream ack patterns, and an integration test that asserts n small writes make it to the client within X ms (ci job).

Mia (support): Customer update: told them short-term mitigations in progress (edge toggle + canary). They accepted canary and are running quick UX checks. Will update thread when they confirm improvement. Thanks all :thumbsup:

Mia (support): Action items summary:
- Jordan: apply `proxy_buffering off` for streaming route (done -> monitor)
- Alex: runtime canary revert flush_ms & disable_chunk_coalesce (in progress)
- Ravi: monitor edge traces + per-route chunk histograms (in progress)
- Mia: coordinate with customer and collect acceptance trace + curl outputs (in progress)

Mia (support): marking this as high-priority escalation. Will reopen if customer still sees p99 regressions after the canary expands.
